Dear all,

First of all, Happy New year to all of you. May 2019 be a prosperous year.

I am writing as I would like your help on the following. I am trying to plot two different ECDF on the same plot in ggplot, based on val and var1. What I would like to do is first to fit a line on those points (of "val" values) and also to colour the points based on var2 (based on taxonomic groups).

2  2 1.0556 log1 algae
3  3 1.3893 log1 algae
4  4 1.3893 log1 algae
5  5 1.4264 log1 algae
6  6 1.4264 log1 algae

$ var2: Factor w/ 9 levels "algae","bivalve",..: 1 1 1 1 1 1 6 6 8 8 …

library(ggplot2)

#create a new dataframe
df<-data.frame(x=c(val), g1=factor(var1), g2=factor(var2)

#plot ecdf
ecd<-ggplot(df, aes(x, colour=g1))+stat_ecdf(geom="point")

I have been able to plot the two different ecdfs but when I try to colour=g2, then I get points everywhere. I also tried to add a geom_line() but without any luck.

I have attached my data in text file (I hope it will go through!)

Thank you very much in advance.

Kind regards,
Maria

messages.body_plain:
Maria,

You could plot the interaction of the two variables.

library(tidyverse)

df1 <- read_tsv("~/Downloads/dat.txt")

ggplot(df1, aes(val)) +

stat_ecdf(geom="point", aes(colour = interaction(var1, var2)))

The trouble here is that you have too many factor levels to plot really.

An alternative would be to facet by one variable or another. Here I'm showing var1:

ggplot(df1, aes(val)) +

stat_ecdf(geom="point", aes(colour = var2)) +

facet_grid(. ~ var1)

This will show you interactions between the different var2 within var1, but comparisons between var1 and var2 by type will be tough.
Faceting the other way is better for looking at comparisons within species type, but poor at comparing by var1:

ggplot(df1, aes(val)) +

stat_ecdf(geom="point", aes(colour = var1)) +

facet_grid(. ~ var2)

You can facet by both variables, but that is essentially one plot per interaction. Code below without picture.

ggplot(df1, aes(val)) +

stat_ecdf(geom="point") +

facet_grid(var1 ~ var2)

HTH,
B

messages.body_plain:
Hi Maria.

To get both the points and the lines for each ecdf by var1, you could just add the ecdf geom twice, once as a line and once as a point, like this:

library(ggplot2)
d = read.table('dat.txt', sep='\t', header=TRUE)
fig = ggplot(d, aes(x=val, fill=var1)) +
  stat_ecdf(aes(color=var1)) +
  stat_ecdf(geom='point', shape='circle filled')
print(fig)

To get the points also colored by var2, the best I could come up with is to compute the ecdf density values separately first and then use them as a new variable for geom_point(). In this case it is probably better to avoid also using color for var1, as this could lead to some confusion about what is represented. You could use the linetype instead. Like this:

d$density = NA
for(i in levels(d$var1)){
  valSubset = d$val[d$var1==i]
  cdfFun = ecdf(valSubset)
  d$density[d$var1==i] = cdfFun(valSubset)
}
fig = ggplot(d, aes(x=val, y=density)) +
  stat_ecdf(aes(lty=var1)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill=var2), shape='circle filled')
print(fig)

There is probably a snazzier way to get the separate density values by var1, mapping or applying function or something. But I'm a bit of an R dinosaur, all loops and ifs.

Luke

Hi Maria.

To get both the points and the lines for each ecdf by var1, you could just add the ecdf geom twice, once as a line and once as a point, like this:

library(ggplot2)
d = read.table('dat.txt', sep='\t', header=TRUE)
fig = ggplot(d, aes(x=val, fill=var1)) +
  stat_ecdf(aes(color=var1)) +
  stat_ecdf(geom='point', shape='circle filled')
print(fig)

To get the points also colored by var2, the best I could come up with is to compute the ecdf density values separately first and then use them as a new variable for geom_point(). In this case it is probably better to avoid also using color for var1, as this could lead to some confusion about what is represented. You could use the linetype instead. Like this:

d$density = NA
for(i in levels(d$var1)){
  valSubset = d$val[d$var1==i]
  cdfFun = ecdf(valSubset)
  d$density[d$var1==i] = cdfFun(valSubset)
}
fig = ggplot(d, aes(x=val, y=density)) +
  stat_ecdf(aes(lty=var1)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill=var2), shape='circle filled')
print(fig)

There is probably a snazzier way to get the separate density values by var1, mapping or applying function or something. But I'm a bit of an R dinosaur, all loops and ifs.

Luke

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

New to this group. Don't make a lot of graphs in my day-to-day work. Need some help making graphs that appear to be a little beyond my current abilities.

Attached is a code file that should help illustrate what I'm trying to accomplish.

I want to create a series of side-by-side graphs for oral chemotherapy among a set of cancer patients. The left side of each graph would show the unprocessed data for a given patient and drug. The right side would show what the data look like after processing. The processing combines overlapping intervals within each drug into a single interval. It then combines non-overlapping intervals that are separated by a sufficiently small amount of time into a single interval. For testing purposes, sufficiently small has been set to <= 63 days (three 21-day cycles).

The first plot generated by the attached code should do a pretty good job of showing what a left-side ought to look like. One of the purposes of this exercise is to depict graphically a specific principle. Specifically, the idea that, if you sequence the start dates and end dates for a set of overlapping intervals, the end of a combined interval will always occur where the number of start dates equals the number of end dates. Hence the counts at the bottom of the graph. Hopefully the graph will help make clear why this should be the case.

The second plot does a less of a good job showing what a right side ought to look like. Hopefully it will be sufficient for practical purposes though. The main deficiency I think is that the scaling for the y-axis is a bit off. If the best way to depict the before and after picture is to have side-by-side graphs, then I imagine the y-axis scaling for the right side will be set to match the y-axis scaling for the left side. Based on what I think I know about ggplot2, it occurred to me that a solution might automatically set the scaling for the y-axis on the right hand side to match that on the left. I could very well be wrong about that though.

One thing I'm struggling with is the scaling of the x-axis on both graphs. In neither case, does it reflect the time/date data. In the first graph, this obscures the fact that only 2 days elapse between 2014-08-04 and 2014-08-06 (which is <= 63). So it might not be immediately intuitive why there is only one interval on the right-hand side and not two.

The x-axis on the right side graph is also showing years and not start dates and end dates.
